reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder combining neonatal cholestasis with chronic lower-limb lymphoedema, described originally in a Norwegian founder population
Cholestasis often presents in the neonatal period with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, pruritus, pale stools, and failure to thrive
The lymphoedema characteristically affects the lower limbs and may not become clinically obvious until later childhood or adolescence
The hepatic component tends to be episodic, with jaundice recurring during infancy and often improving with age, though some progress to fibrosis
The disorder maps to a locus on chromosome 15 (LCS1); the precise gene and mechanism linking hepatic and lymphatic disease remain incompletely defined
Fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption is common, so serum bile acids are raised and vitamins A, D, E, and K should be monitored and replaced
Management is supportive: ursodeoxycholic acid for cholestasis, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, nutritional support, and physical/compression therapy for lymphoedema
reference.pathophysiology: Aagenaes syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition characterised by generalised hypoplasia of lymphatic vessels together with intrahepatic cholestasis. A defect in lymphatic development is thought to impair drainage from the liver and lower limbs, and reduced hepatic lymph flow may contribute to the cholestasis and periportal fibrosis. The causative gene has not been definitively identified, though linkage studies place the locus (LCS1) on chromosome 15q. Cholestatic episodes tend to be most severe in infancy and to lessen over time, whereas the peripheral lymphoedema is progressive and lifelong.
additionalDifferentials: Primary lymphoedema (Milroy or Meige disease) without hepatic involvement
additionalInvestigations: Serum bile acids and fractionated (conjugated) bilirubin
Liver function tests including gamma-glutamyl transferase and transaminases
Fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E) and coagulation studies for vitamin K status
Liver biopsy showing cholestasis with variable portal fibrosis and giant-cell change
Lymphoscintigraphy or imaging to demonstrate lymphatic hypoplasia
Genetic testing and family/pedigree analysis, particularly in individuals of Norwegian ancestry
redFlags: Vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy causing bleeding in a cholestatic infant
Progressive hepatic fibrosis or signs of portal hypertension
Failure to thrive with severe fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Cellulitis or recurrent infection complicating chronic lymphoedema
reference.prognosis: The cholestatic episodes are often most troublesome in infancy and tend to improve with age, and many patients have a near-normal lifespan; however, a minority develop chronic liver disease or cirrhosis, and the lower-limb lymphoedema is lifelong and can be disabling.
pitfalls: Overlooking lymphoedema when it is subtle in infancy and only becomes apparent years after the hepatic presentation
Attributing recurrent neonatal jaundice to common causes without considering an inherited cholestatic syndrome
Neglecting fat-soluble vitamin monitoring, leading to preventable coagulopathy or rickets
Assuming a good hepatic outcome in every case and missing progression to fibrosis
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Suchy, Sokol & Balistreri, Liver Disease in Children
